title: Basic directions, reduced costs, and the ratio test

sections.body_md:
A basic feasible solution sits at a corner. A neighboring corner is reached by raising one nonbasic variable and adjusting the basic variables so the equalities still hold. If the entering index is \(j\), the direction \(d\) has a 1 in position \(j\), zeros in the other nonbasic positions, and basic part \(d_B = -B^{-1} A_j\). Then \(A d = 0\), so \(x + \theta d\) stays on the affine set for every step \(\theta\).

The objective changes at the rate \(c^T d\). That rate is the reduced cost \(\bar{c}_j = c_j - c_B^T B^{-1} A_j\). For a minimization, a negative reduced cost means the objective falls as \(\theta\) grows. The step cannot grow forever unless \(d_B\) has no negative component. If some basic coordinate of \(d\) is negative, that coordinate hits zero at a finite step. The longest feasible step is the smallest of those hitting times. That minimum is the ratio test.

If \(d_B \ge 0\) and the reduced cost is negative, every positive step is feasible and the objective is unbounded below. The sign of the reduced cost and the sign pattern of the direction answer different questions: one is about the objective, and the other is about staying inside \(x \ge 0\).

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
The reduced cost and the step are
\[
\bar{c}_j = c_j - c_B^T B^{-1} A_j, \qquad \theta = \min_{i : \bar{a}_{ij} > 0} \frac{\bar{b}_i}{\bar{a}_{ij}},
\]
where \(\bar{a}_j = B^{-1} A_j\) and \(\bar{b} = B^{-1} b\). The basic direction is \(d_B = -\bar{a}_j\). On a single row with multiplier \(u\) and column entry \(a\), the reduced cost collapses to \(c - u a\). The objective change on a feasible step is \(\theta \bar{c}_j\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Minimize \(-6x - y\) subject to \(x + y + s = 9\) and \(x + 2y + t = 17\), starting from the slack basis \(s = 9\), \(t = 17\). The basic cost is zero, so the reduced costs are \(-6\) and \(-1\). Enter \(x\). Its column is \((1, 1)\), and the ratios are \(9/1\) and \(17/1\). The step is 9.

The lane step cuts 54. The objective change is \(9 \cdot (-6) = -54\), so the cost falls by 54. The new point has \(x = 9\) and \(t = 8\), with \(s\) at zero. Entering \(y\) instead would also decrease the cost, at the slower rate \(-1\). Either choice is a descent step. The more negative rate is a pivot rule, not a requirement for correctness of the direction.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Taking the largest ratio instead of the smallest drives some basic variable negative. The test wants the first hitting time, which is the minimum. A second miss is to divide by a nonpositive column entry. Those rows do not block the step. A third is to read a negative reduced cost as unboundedness. Unboundedness also needs a direction that never goes negative. A fourth is to insist on the most negative reduced cost. Any negative reduced cost gives a feasible descent direction. The choice among them changes the path and not the sign of the slope.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: One simplex iteration packages this arithmetic: price the nonbasic columns, stop if every reduced cost is nonnegative, otherwise enter one negative column, stop if the ratio test finds no positive entry, and otherwise pivot on a minimum-ratio row. Repeating that iteration walks along edges. The first basis, when the slack basis is not feasible, comes from an auxiliary problem whose own reduced costs are computed in the same way.
